1338.title: Tendai
1338.hook: the Japanese form of Tiantai on Mount Hiei, home of many founders
1338.howItsDone: Tendai Buddhists in Japan study the Lotus Sutra and combine meditation, precepts, esoteric ritual and recitation of Amida Buddha's name; Mount Hiei remains the school's center of training.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the golden lion: one gold, one shape, not two. Your line: gold and lion. A new week, and the path crosses the sea.

Honen. Shinran. Eisai. Dogen. Nichiren. Say those names to someone who knows Japanese Buddhism and they'll hear founders: the Pure Land schools, Zen lines, the Nichiren schools. Teachers who went in different directions and sometimes argued hard. Now ask where each of them began. Tradition gives the same answer again and again: a forested mountain above Kyoto, where they studied as young monks before they ever founded anything. One slope, many roads leading down from it. The school on that slope is the Japanese form of the Tiantai from this week: Tendai.
screen: `FOUNDERS IN MANY DIRECTIONS.` → `WHERE DID EACH BEGIN?` → `ONE SLOPE, MANY ROADS.`

segments.voice: A Japanese monk named Saicho traveled to China, studied the Tiantai teaching, and brought it home to Mount Hiei; in Japanese the name is said Tendai. This path met Saicho and his mountain before. Today's question is a different one: what did the school hold, that so many roads could come out of it? Tendai kept the Lotus Sutra at its center, as Tiantai did. But on Mount Hiei the monks also trained in meditation, kept the monastic precepts, practiced esoteric ritual with mantras and mandalas, and chanted the name of Amida Buddha. All under one roof: less a single practice than a whole curriculum, a rope of many strands. Later teachers who trained there each, in his own way, took hold of one strand and found the whole rope in it. Honen and Shinran took the calling of Amida's name. Eisai and Dogen took meditation, and brought Zen lineages back from China. Nichiren took the Lotus Sutra itself. Their schools have their own stories, and the path will reach them soon. Tradition calls Mount Hiei the mother mountain of Japanese Buddhism. A mother isn't the same as her children, and children don't always agree with their mother, or with each other; some of these founders left the mountain in sharp disagreement. But the name holds something true: they learned to read, chant and sit in the same place. And Tendai didn't vanish when its children left. It is still practiced on the mountain today, holding many strands at once.
screen: `SAICHO CARRIES TIANTAI HOME.` · `MANY STRANDS UNDER ONE ROOF.` · `EACH FOUNDER TAKES ONE STRAND.` · `A MOTHER, NOT A COPY.` · then, large: `THE MOTHER MOUNTAIN.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind a place that taught you before you went your own way, a school, a kitchen, a first job, a team, a congregation, a family, whether you left it gladly or arguing. Let one thing it gave you come up, a habit, a skill, a way of standing, and hold it for a few breaths. If you'd like, bow your head slightly toward it, inside.

1339.title: Shingon
1339.hook: Kukai's esoteric school: mantra, mudra and mandala
1339.howItsDone: Shingon Buddhists practice under a teacher, joining mudras of the hands, the recitation of mantras and meditation on mandalas; deeper practices are given only after initiation.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Tendai and Mount Hiei. Your line: the mother mountain. Today, a second Japanese school, on a different mountain.

A young Japanese monk arrives at a temple in the Chinese capital, a long way from home. He's come to find a teacher. The master of the place is, the story says, not well. When the visitor is brought in, the old man smiles and says something like: I knew you were coming, and I've been waiting a long time. Then, instead of testing him for years, he begins handing over everything he knows. The visitor is Kukai, and the story comes from Kukai's own report home. The teaching he carried back became a school: Shingon.
screen: `A TEACHER WHO WAS WAITING.` → `EVERYTHING, HANDED OVER.` → `KUKAI CARRIES IT HOME.`

segments.voice: Shingon means true word, the Japanese rendering of mantra. This path met Kukai before, on the pilgrim's road and on his mountain, Koyasan. Today, what he taught there. Shingon teaches through body, speech and mind together, and calls them the three mysteries. The body forms a mudra, a gesture of the hands. The speech recites a mantra, a sacred sound. The mind rests on a mandala, or on a single buddha pictured within it. In Shingon's teaching, these aren't three tricks for getting somewhere. They are the Buddha's own body, speech and mind meeting the practitioner's. Kukai wrote an essay on becoming a buddha in this very body. Some Buddhists of his day spoke of awakening as the end of a road many lifetimes long. Kukai's claim was bolder: when the practitioner's gestures, words and thoughts are joined with the Buddha's, awakening is possible here, in this life, in this body. Why is it called esoteric? Esoteric means hidden, or inner. In Shingon, these practices are passed on from teacher to student after the student has been prepared, the way the old master in China handed them to Kukai. So you'll hear Shingon described from the outside, as here, more than you'll see it explained in public; the hands, the sound and the mind are learned in person. What anyone can notice is the idea underneath: body, speech and mind aren't obstacles to awakening. In Shingon, they're the doors.

segments.voice: Nothing secret, just a simple gesture used in Buddhist meditation: rest one hand in the other in your lap, palms up, the thumb tips touching lightly, as if holding a sheet of paper between them. If the thumbs press hard, you're tense; if they drift apart, you're drifting. Let the gesture tell you how the mind is doing, and come back to it each time.

1340.title: Two mandalas
1340.hook: the womb-world and diamond-world mandalas, hung side by side
1340.howItsDone: In Shingon temples the womb-world and diamond-world mandalas are commonly hung as a pair; in initiation, the student casts a flower onto a mandala to form a bond with a buddha, and practitioners meditate on both.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Shingon, Kukai's school of hand, sound and mind. Your line: true word. Today, what hangs on the walls of a Shingon hall.

A blindfold goes on. The young monk is led forward in the dim hall and handed a single flower. In front of him, laid out flat, is a great painted mandala, crowded with buddhas, though he can't see any of them. He's told to let the flower go. It drops. Wherever it lands, that figure becomes his link to the whole teaching. Kukai's own report home says that when he did this in China, his flower fell on the great Buddha at the center, and not once but twice, on two different mandalas. Those two are today's word.
screen: `A BLINDFOLD AND A FLOWER.` → `WHEREVER IT LANDS.` → `KUKAI'S FLOWER, TWICE.`

segments.voice: Here a mandala isn't a pretty pattern. It's a map of awakening, painted: buddhas and bodhisattvas set out in their places around a center. In Shingon, the center of both is Mahavairocana, the great sun Buddha, called Dainichi in Japanese. One mandala is named for the womb. At its heart is a lotus in bloom with Mahavairocana in the middle, and figures open out from it, court around court, like petals, like a family. Shingon teachers link it with compassion, and with the way awakening is already present in all things, the way a child is held in a womb before it's born. The other is named for the diamond, or thunderbolt, the thing that cannot be broken. It's laid out as a grid of squares, each square its own assembly of buddhas. Shingon teachers link it with wisdom, sharp and unbreakable, the mind that sees clearly. In Shingon halls the two often hang facing each other, or on either side of the altar. And here is the point of the pair. Shingon teaches that they are two, and not two: compassion and wisdom, the world as it is and the mind that knows it. Neither is the real one with the other as decoration. A practitioner sits between them, in the middle, and practice is the work of letting the two meet. Some readers take Kukai's flower, falling on the center of each, as a sign that he would hold both together.
screen: `A MAP OF AWAKENING, PAINTED.` · `THE WOMB WORLD: A LOTUS, COMPASSION.` · `THE DIAMOND WORLD: A GRID, WISDOM.` · `TWO, AND NOT TWO.` · then, large: `TWO WORLDS.`

segments.voice: Find a pair near you, your two hands, two windows, two shoes by the door, and let your eyes rest on one, then the other, noticing how each is different: shape, wear, which way it faces. Then notice how they belong together, each making sense next to the other, and breathe with both in view.
Two mandalas. The womb world and the diamond world of Shingon, compassion and wisdom, hung side by side and taught as two and not two. Today's word.

1341.title: The letter A
1341.hook: Shingon meditation on the Sanskrit letter A, the sound of all beginnings
1341.howItsDone: Shingon practitioners practice ajikan, contemplating the Siddham letter A on a moon disc above a lotus while breathing and sounding A; it is also taught to lay people as an introduction to Shingon meditation.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the two mandalas, womb and diamond. Your line: two worlds. Today, Shingon shrinks the whole map down to a single letter.

Ah. Open your mouth and let the breath out, and that's the sound that comes. No tongue against teeth, no lips pressing. Babies make it. Doctors ask for it with a little wooden stick. People sigh it when the hot bath is just right. It might be the plainest sound a person can make. Shingon took that sound, and the letter that writes it, and set it at the center of a meditation: a single letter on a white moon, on a lotus. That letter is today's word: A.
screen: `AH: THE PLAINEST SOUND.` → `NO TONGUE, NO LIPS.` → `A LETTER ON A MOON.`

segments.voice: Shingon teachers point out that in the Indian alphabet A stands first, and that every consonant is read with a hidden a sound after it unless a mark silences it. So the A, they say, is in every sound, the way the open breath is underneath every word. The Mahavairocana Sutra, which Shingon treasures, links the letter A with the teaching that all things are unborn from the beginning. Shingon reads it this way: before any thing appears, before any word is shaped, there is an origin that was never made and never ends. The A points to it, and the plainest sound becomes a sign for the ground of everything. The practice is called ajikan, contemplation of the letter A. Tradition associates it with Kukai's school, and the image is simple: a lotus; on the lotus, a full moon disc, white and round; on the moon, the letter A, written in an old Indian script. The practitioner gazes at the image, breathes, and lets the sound and the shape of A fill the mind, until the moon seems to grow, and the letter with it. Why so small? Yesterday's mandalas were crowded with buddhas, a whole world painted. Today's is one letter. In Shingon, both carry the whole teaching. The vast map and the single sound are not two, the way the womb world and the diamond world are not two. A person who can't take in a whole mandala can still breathe out ah.

segments.voice: Take a slow breath in, and on the out-breath let the sound come, quietly or only in your mind: ah, as long as the breath is and no longer. Breathe in again, and again, ah, and if you'd like, picture a round white moon in front of you as you do it. If you lose the sound, start the next breath fresh; there's nothing to get right.
The letter A. In Shingon, the first letter and the sound inside every sound, a sign that all things are unborn from the beginning, and the heart of ajikan. Today's word.

1342.title: The Nichiren schools
1342.hook: many schools follow Nichiren's focus on the Lotus Sutra's title
1342.howItsDone: Nichiren Buddhists chant the title of the Lotus Sutra, nam myoho renge kyo (or namu myoho renge kyo), often with palms together before a scroll, alone or together in temples and homes.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the letter A: Shingon's plainest sound, set on a moon as a sign of what was never born. Your line: ah.

A low, steady sound comes through an apartment door, the same words over and over, like a train on a long track. Nam myoho renge kyo. Inside, a few neighbors sit side by side, palms together, facing a small wooden cabinet. It sounds like a mantra, and in a way it works like one. But it's something more surprising: a title. The name of a book, said out loud, with a word of devotion in front. A whole family of Buddhist schools grew up around saying that name.
screen: `A SOUND THROUGH A DOOR.` → `NAM MYOHO RENGE KYO.` → `IT IS A TITLE.`

segments.voice: You met Nichiren on day one thousand; today, the family that grew from him. First, the man. Nichiren was a Japanese monk who trained in Tendai, where the Lotus Sutra was already held in honor. Tradition says he studied widely and came away convinced that the Lotus Sutra was the heart of the Buddha's teaching, and that his country needed to turn back to it. He said so loudly, and in the stories his followers tell, he paid for it with exile and danger. Second, the big idea. Nichiren taught that the title isn't just a label on the cover. It holds the whole sutra, the way a seed holds a tree. So saying it with faith takes in the entire teaching at once. The practice is called daimoku, the title. Third, the words. Myoho renge kyo is the Japanese reading of the sutra's name: the wonderful dharma, the lotus flower, the sutra. In front goes namu, or nam, a word of devotion, something like I give myself to. In Sanskrit the sutra is the Saddharma Pundarika, the lotus of the true dharma. Some communities chant nam, others namu: same title, a different breath. Fourth, what came after. Nichiren's disciples and their students built many schools and lineages. Some are temple traditions with priests; some are lay movements that meet in living rooms. They share the sutra and the chant, and they disagree, sometimes sharply, about other things, which the next few days take up. What they hold in common: a few words, said out loud and meant, can open the Buddha's teaching right inside an ordinary life.

1343.title: The written mandala
1343.hook: Nichiren's scroll, inscribed with the title and the names of Buddhas
1343.howItsDone: Nichiren Buddhists enshrine a gohonzon, a scroll with the Lotus Sutra's title down the center and the names of Buddhas and other beings around it, and chant facing it, often morning and evening, at home and in temples.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Nichiren schools, and a chant that turns out to be a book's title. Your line: the title.

Open the doors of the small cabinet, and there's no statue inside. There's a sheet of paper, mounted as a scroll. Down the middle runs a column of large, bold brushstrokes. Around it, smaller columns spread toward the edges, like a crowd gathered around a speaker. Some marks near the sides look less like writing than drawing. People bow to this paper, chant facing it, and dust the cabinet that holds it. The scroll has a name: gohonzon.
screen: `NO STATUE INSIDE.` → `A COLUMN OF BOLD STROKES.` → `A CROWD OF NAMES.`

segments.voice: First, what it is. Gohonzon means, roughly, the object of devotion, said with respect. Nichiren inscribed scrolls like this by hand and gave them to his followers. Where other temples carved or painted the Buddha, he wrote, which is why some call it a written mandala: a sacred diagram made of words instead of pictures. Second, the center. Down the middle, in the largest letters, runs yesterday's title, namu myoho renge kyo, with Nichiren's own signature below it. The title is the heart of the scroll, as it is the heart of the chant. Third, everything around it. The Lotus Sutra tells of a great jeweled tower that rises out of the earth and hangs in the air. Inside sits a Buddha from an age long past, and Shakyamuni Buddha sits down beside him while a vast assembly gathers to listen. The gohonzon is often read as that scene, written out: two Buddhas' names on either side of the title, and around them bodhisattvas, disciples, gods and guardians, even beings from the dark and troubled corners of existence. Even the dark corners have a place on the page. Fourth, how people use it. Practitioners chant facing it, often morning and evening. Some communities describe it as a kind of mirror: chanting before it, a person is meant to see their own capacity for awakening reflected back. Communities differ, sometimes deeply, about which scrolls are authentic and who may give them out, and that's tomorrow. But the scroll is handled with care: kept clean, set up high, never tossed aside.

segments.voice: Face a sacred scroll, verse or image if there's one where you live, or else any page of writing that matters to you: a letter or a card. Look at it without reading it, noticing where your eye lands first, what sits at the center and what sits out at the edges. Then close your eyes, keep the picture in mind, and ask quietly what you would place at the center of your own page.
Gohonzon. The scroll Nichiren inscribed, with the Lotus Sutra's title down the center and the names of Buddhas and many beings around it, faced in chanting. Today's word.
Your line: the scroll. Words, not a statue, at the center of the room. Same time tomorrow.

1344.title: Many Nichiren communities
1344.hook: Nichiren Shu, Nichiren Shoshu, Soka Gakkai and others differ in important ways; each speaks for itself
1344.howItsDone: Nichiren Buddhists belong to several communities, among them Nichiren Shu, Nichiren Shoshu and Soka Gakkai, which share the Lotus Sutra and the chanted title but differ on Nichiren's role, the gohonzon and the place of priests and laypeople.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the gohonzon: the written mandala, the title down its center and a whole assembly around it. Your line: the scroll.

Ask a handful of Nichiren Buddhists who Nichiren was, which scroll matters most and who keeps the teaching, and the answers won't all match. Each will be sincere. Each will come with reasons, and a history of its own. A fair listener's first job is a plain one: let each answer finish before reaching for a verdict. That's today, and it closes a week among Japan's temple schools, from Tendai's mountain to Shingon's mandalas to the chanted title.
screen: `THE ANSWERS DON'T ALL MATCH.` → `LET EACH ONE FINISH.` → `A WEEK IN JAPAN'S SCHOOLS.`

segments.voice: Here are three, each as it describes itself, none ranked. First, Nichiren Shu. It sees itself as carrying on the temple lineages of Nichiren's disciples. It honors Nichiren as a great teacher and bodhisattva sent to spread the Lotus Sutra, and places Shakyamuni, the eternal Buddha of the Lotus Sutra, at the center of devotion. Its temples may hold statues as well as scrolls, and its members often chant namu myoho renge kyo. Second, Nichiren Shoshu. It traces its line through Nikko, one of Nichiren's senior disciples, to a head temple at the foot of Mount Fuji, Taiseki-ji. It teaches that Nichiren himself is the true Buddha for this age, and reveres one great scroll kept at the head temple as the heart of its faith. Its priests confer the gohonzon on members. Third, Soka Gakkai. It began in Japan as a society of lay educators connected to Nichiren Shoshu. The two later parted ways, and the separation still matters to both. Soka Gakkai now describes itself as a lay Buddhist movement, with members far beyond Japan, built on chanting, study and small discussion meetings in members' homes, and on work for peace, culture and education. And there are others: Rissho Kosei-kai, Reiyukai, and the monks of Nipponzan Myohoji, who walk beating drums and build peace pagodas. Each is a sangha, and each claims to be faithful to Nichiren. They differ on who he was, which scroll is true, and whether priests or laypeople carry the teaching. Those aren't small questions, which is exactly why each deserves to be heard in its own voice, not through a rival's summary, and not through mine.

segments.voice: Choose one community from today, recall one thing it says about itself in its own words, and hold that sentence for a few breaths without adding a but. Then think of a group you belong to, a family, a team, a faith, a town, and the first sentence you'd want a stranger to hear about it. Sit with the two sentences side by side.
Many Nichiren communities. Nichiren Shu, Nichiren Shoshu, Soka Gakkai and others: one chant, one sutra, and real differences, each explained in its own voice. Today's word.
Your line: each speaks for itself. A fair hearing comes before any verdict. Until tomorrow.
